query: For additively manufactured high-entropy-alloy components, what single intervention could improve dimensional precision and mechanical integrity while reducing fabrication-induced defects? Formulate one hypothesis that identifies the intervention, explains its mechanism, predicts the improvement relative to the current fabrication baseline, defines the processing and application conditions under which it should hold, identifies supporting prior evidence, and proposes an experiment whose result would falsify the hypothesis.

generation.hypothesis: In laser powder bed fusion (LPBF) of face-centered cubic (FCC) high-entropy alloys, adding a low-energy, high-speed interlayer laser remelting pass after each layer will simultaneously improve dimensional precision and mechanical integrity by reducing fabrication-induced defects through capillary-driven pore collapse and surface smoothing, without degrading strength.
generation.material_initial_state: Additively manufactured FCC high-entropy alloy (e.g., CoCrFeMnNi family) built by LPBF using a standard single-exposure hatch and perimeter scan per layer, inert Ar atmosphere, no in situ remelt, no hot isostatic pressing, with typical as-built defects (keyhole/lack-of-fusion pores, surface asperities, spatter adhesion, residual stress).
generation.intervention: Introduce an in situ, layer-by-layer laser remelting pass that scans the just-solidified layer at high speed with reduced linear energy density (approximately 30–60% of the main hatch linear energy density), covering both hatch and perimeters with a rotated scan vector, to shallowly re-melt and reflow the surface without deep keyholing.
generation.conditions: LPBF in conduction-mode parameter window (to avoid keyholing) with 20–40 μm layer thickness, hatch spacing near one half to one melt-pool width, inert gas O2 < 100 ppm, baseplate preheat 100–300 °C, particle size 15–45 μm, wall features ≥ 2 melt-pool widths, scan speed and power chosen so the remelt depth is < 0.5 of the prior melt-pool depth. Applicable to FCC HEAs with moderate solidification range (e.g., CoCrFeMnNi variants).
generation.structural_mediator: Reduced lack-of-fusion and keyhole porosity via capillary backfilling during remelt; smoother surfaces and perimeters from viscous reflow and improved wetting of partially fused particles; attenuated residual stress from local thermal relaxation; modest homogenization of microsegregation at cell boundaries.
generation.mechanism: A shallow, low-energy remelt reflows the recently solidified layer, allowing capillary pressure to collapse and heal subsurface pores and fuse partially melted particles, while smoothing asperities and reducing spatter attachment. The secondary thermal cycle lowers effective cooling rate locally, reducing thermal gradients and stress concentrators that nucleate microcracks. Perimeter remelting improves edge wetting and dimensional fidelity by trimming balling and partially sintered powder. The net effect is fewer and smaller internal defects and smoother perimeters, mediating enhanced mechanical integrity and dimensional precision.
generation.predicted_outcome: Relative to the same build without interlayer remelting: (1) lower mean porosity volume fraction and a shift to smaller pore sizes; (2) reduced mean surface roughness on up-facing and side surfaces; (3) reduced mean absolute deviation from CAD on representative features (walls, holes) and lower out-of-plane distortion; (4) increased tensile ductility and fatigue life at room temperature, with yield strength maintained within experimental scatter. Effects are expected to be modest-to-moderate but directionally positive under the stated conditions.
generation.baseline: Standard single-pass-per-layer LPBF process of the same HEA powder and build layout, same hatch/perimeter parameters, gas flow, and preheat, but without any interlayer remelt pass.
generation.boundary: Benefits may diminish or invert if: (a) remelt energy is too high (induces keyholing, evaporation, spatter, or over-melting of fine features) or too low (insufficient reflow); (b) alloys with high hot-cracking susceptibility (e.g., some Al- or refractory-rich HEAs) experience liquation cracking during remelt; (c) extremely thin features (< 2 melt-pool widths) are over-thinned by remelt; (d) severe heat accumulation in massive sections negates stress relief benefits; (e) environments with elevated oxygen promote oxide films that hinder wetting; (f) non-LPBF processes (e.g., EBM, DED) where thermal histories and defect modes differ.
generation.uncertainty: Optimal remelt energy density and scan strategy will vary with alloy composition and geometry; the balance between pore healing and potential grain coarsening is alloy- and parameter-dependent; the magnitude of improvement in dimensional precision and mechanical integrity is uncertain without alloy- and geometry-specific calibration; throughput penalties and thermal accumulation effects may constrain applicability to large parts.

falsification_experiment.design: Print two cohorts of identical coupons (e.g., tensile bars, wall and hole features, and fatigue specimens) from the same FCC HEA powder in one build: baseline (no remelt) and interlayer-remelt (same parameters plus the specified low-energy remelt after each layer). Keep gas flow, preheat, and layout identical. Use n ≥ 10 specimens per cohort for each test type to enable statistical comparison.
measurements: X-ray computed tomography to quantify porosity volume fraction and pore size distribution in gauge and bulk regions
3D optical or CMM metrology to quantify mean absolute dimensional deviation from CAD for walls, holes, and overall flatness/warpage
Surface roughness (Sa or Ra) on up-facing and side surfaces via confocal or stylus profilometry
Residual stress by X-ray diffraction on as-built surfaces
Room-temperature uniaxial tensile testing (yield strength, UTS, uniform elongation, total elongation)
High-cycle or rotating-bending fatigue life at a fixed stress amplitude, or S–N curves
Metallography/EBSD to assess melt-pool geometry, grain structure, and evidence of remelt depth; EDS mapping for segregation at cell boundaries
falsification_experiment.falsification_rule: The hypothesis is falsified if, compared to baseline, the remelt cohort fails to show statistically significant (p < 0.05) reductions in both (i) mean porosity volume fraction and (ii) mean absolute dimensional deviation, and also fails to reduce mean surface roughness; or if there is a statistically significant degradation (p < 0.05) in tensile ductility (uniform or total elongation) or fatigue life at a given stress level.
